paras: The attempted lynching of George Berry took place at Texarkana, Arkansas, on December 30, 1881, when railroad men took Berry from officers who were bringing him to jail and tried to hang him for the shooting of John Smith. The hanging failed because the cotton scales they used were too low, and the men handed Berry back to the officers while vowing to hang him if Smith died. The story ran by telegraph in papers from Richmond to Los Angeles, most of which predicted a lynching that night.

According to a Texarkana special to the Little Rock Gazette, Smith was shot and mortally wounded at two o'clock in the morning by Berry, a man he had never seen before. The Dallas Herald's correspondent described Smith as "a hardworking railroad man" and Berry as "a rowdy and a bad character generally," and cited witnesses who called the shooting "a cowardly and unprovoked murder." None of the reports gives the race of either man.

Berry was arrested, by the Herald's account "last night," and while officers were taking him to jail a group of railroad men took him from them. The men tried to hang him on a pair of cotton scales, but the scales were too low, and they gave him back to the officers. In the Gazette's version they declared that they would hang Berry that night if Smith died, while the Herald quoted them as saying he "should swing before sundown."
Neither report says where the scales stood, whether Berry was moved there from the place where he was seized, or how many men took part.

On December 30 Smith was reported to be dying, and the Herald's correspondent wrote that "we expect a lynching to-night." No report of Smith's death, of a second attempt on Berry, of an inquest, or of a trial was found in coverage through January 1882.

The Gazette's special, sent from Little Rock, carried the story east and south on December 31, appearing in the Savannah Morning News as "Cotton Scales for a Gallows," in the New-York Tribune as "An Attempt at Lynching," and in the Richmond Dispatch as "An Unprovoked Murder." Other dailies in Knoxville, Wheeling and Memphis printed the same text, and the St. Paul Daily Globe ran it on New Year's Day under the head "Judge Lynch." In the West a one-line brief described Berry as "a bad character" who "will probably be lynched," headed "A Candidate for Judge Lynch" in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union.

The Dallas Herald gave the story the most pointed treatment, headlining the "Cowardly Murder of an Inoffensive Railroad Man at Texarkana Yesterday by a Brutal Ruffian" who "Barely Escapes Lynching" at the hands of railway employees. The Herald reprinted its special in its weekly edition of January 5, 1882. Across these versions the papers treated the shooting as an unprovoked murder and a lynching as likely, without criticism of the men who tried to hang Berry; only the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer's digest called them "a mob" and "lynchers."

A separate Texarkana special to the Galveston News, printed in the Memphis Daily Appeal, told a different story: a "cowboy named Tom Barry" abused Smith, "a laborer," in front of a saloon and shot him when Smith turned to defend himself. In that version "the citizens" seized Barry and put a rope about his neck, and the city marshal prevented the lynching and took him to jail. The Gazette and Herald texts are nearly identical and may share a source, so the News special is the only clearly independent account.

The accused's name also varied, printed as John Berry in the New-York Tribune and as George Beery or Barry in the Lancaster digest, which placed Texarkana in Texas. The St. Paul Daily Globe gave the time of the shooting as two in the afternoon rather than two in the morning.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of George Berry
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Railroad men took the accused from officers and tried to hang him, then returned him while threatening to hang him if his alleged victim died, an attempted lynching (A4, A6, A8).

The men who seized Berry acted without authority to punish an alleged shooting, but the hanging failed and he was handed back alive (A4, A6, A8); no report of his later death was found, and the group's size is given only as 'railroad men', 'citizens' or 'a mob' (A4, A8, A10).

The Gazette's and the Herald's Texarkana specials and a separate Galveston News special agree that Smith was shot and that men seized the accused and tried to hang him before he went to jail (A4, A6, A8), though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Little Rock Gazette's Texarkana special (wire)
accounts.gist: Berry shot Smith at 2 a.m. without provocation; on the way to jail railroad men took him from officers and tried to hang him on cotton scales, which were too low, and returned him, vowing to hang him that night if Smith died.

accounts.label: Dallas Herald's own Texarkana special
accounts.gist: Matches the Gazette text nearly word for word, adding that the men said he 'should swing before sundown' if Smith died that day and that 'we expect a lynching to-night'.

accounts.label: Galveston News's Texarkana special
accounts.gist: A cowboy named Tom Barry abused Smith in front of a saloon and shot him when Smith turned to defend himself; citizens put a rope about Barry's neck, but the city marshal prevented the lynching and jailed him.

framing.detail: The Dallas Herald headlined a 'Cowardly Murder of an Inoffensive Railroad Man ... by a Brutal Ruffian' who 'Barely Escapes Lynching' and wrote 'we expect a lynching to-night', without criticizing the mob.
Eastern and Southern dailies ran the Gazette special under heads such as 'Cotton Scales for a Gallows', 'An Attempt at Lynching', 'An Unprovoked Murder' and 'Judge Lynch'.
Western papers ran a one-line brief calling Berry 'a bad character' who 'will probably be lynched', one headed 'A Candidate for Judge Lynch'.

conflicts.note: Variant spellings of one accused across wire versions; the Gazette text most often gives George Berry.

info: Shooting at 2 a.m. on December 30, 1881, followed by the attempt to hang the accused while he was being taken to jail; one reprint prints 'afternoon'.
Texarkana; the attempt was made on the way to jail, using a pair of cotton scales; the shooting took place in front of a saloon per the News special.
Target of the mob: George (Geo.) Berry; also printed 'John Berry', 'George Beery'/'Barry', and 'Tom Barry'. No race stated in any report.
Accused of shooting and mortally wounding John Smith (also 'John R. Smith', 'Jno. Smith'), described as a hardworking railroad man or a laborer, whom witnesses said he had never seen before.
'Railroad men' (Gazette, Herald); 'the citizens' (News special); 'a mob' and 'lynchers' (Lancaster digest).
Berry returned to officers alive; the papers predicted a lynching that night if Smith died; no later report of Smith's death, a lynching, or a trial was found.
